slides.title: Four senses of one term
slides.text: The term 'INTERNATIONAL CRIMINAL LAW' SUFFERS FROM CONSIDERABLE AMBIGUITY, and Kreß distinguishes FOUR principal senses. YOU MUST BE ABLE TO TELL THEM APART, BECAUSE THE WHOLE ARTICLE IS BUILT ON THE DISTINCTION. 1) THE LAW GOVERNING THE PRESCRIPTIVE CRIMINAL JURISDICTION OF STATES — that is, domestic rules on the (extra)territorial reach of criminal law, plus the limits international law places on it; it therefore consists of NATIONAL AND INTERNATIONAL RULES ALIKE. 2) THE LAW OF INTERNATIONAL COOPERATION IN CRIMINAL MATTERS. 3) TRANSNATIONAL CRIMINAL LAW — the body of treaties on crimes of a cross-border nature. 4) INTERNATIONAL CRIMINAL LAW STRICTO SENSU (and supranational criminal law) — which establishes INDIVIDUAL CRIMINAL RESPONSIBILITY DIRECTLY UNDER INTERNATIONAL LAW.

cards.q: Name the four senses of the term 'international criminal law'.
cards.a: 1) The law governing the PRESCRIPTIVE CRIMINAL JURISDICTION OF STATES (domestic rules on the reach of criminal law plus the limits of international law). 2) The law of INTERNATIONAL COOPERATION in criminal matters. 3) TRANSNATIONAL criminal law (treaties on cross-border crimes). 4) International criminal law STRICTO SENSU, which establishes individual criminal responsibility directly under international law.

slides.title: Principles of criminal jurisdiction and forms of cooperation
slides.text: The principles of the first sense: TERRITORIALITY, ACTIVE AND PASSIVE PERSONALITY, THE PROTECTIVE PRINCIPLE (possibly including the 'effects doctrine'), THE PRINCIPLE OF VICARIOUS CRIMINAL JURISDICTION and UNIVERSAL JURISDICTION. And a distinction worth having: WHILE THE PRINCIPLE OF TERRITORIALITY IS OBSERVED BY ALL STATES AND IS UNCONTESTED IN INTERNATIONAL LAW, PRACTICE VARIES ON THE OTHERS AND THEIR LEGALITY IS MORE OR LESS DISPUTED. Cooperation in criminal matters means THE DELIBERATE PROVISION OF SUPPORT TO CRIMINAL PROCEEDINGS IN ANOTHER FORUM. Between states three forms were originally distinguished: EXTRADITION of a person for prosecution or for the execution of a sentence; TRANSIT of a person through a third state; and MUTUAL ASSISTANCE, chiefly comprising THE OBTAINING OF EVIDENCE. In time the TRANSFER OF A PERSON FOR THE EXECUTION OF A SENTENCE became separate, and the more recent additions are the TRANSFER OF CRIMINAL PROCEEDINGS and so-called 'PASSIVE COOPERATION', in which the requested state permits the requesting state to carry out procedural acts. THE MOST RECENT DEVELOPMENT IS COOPERATION BETWEEN STATES AND INTERNATIONAL CRIMINAL COURTS — increasingly described as VERTICAL as against the HORIZONTAL cooperation between states.

terms.def: Vertical is cooperation between a state and an international criminal court; horizontal is between states.

cards.q: Name the principles of criminal jurisdiction and say which is uncontested.
cards.a: Territoriality, active and passive personality, the protective principle (possibly including the effects doctrine), vicarious jurisdiction and universal jurisdiction. ONLY TERRITORIALITY IS UNCONTESTED AND UNIVERSALLY OBSERVED; on the others state practice varies and their legality under international law is more or less disputed.

cards.q: What is vertical cooperation in criminal matters?
cards.a: Cooperation between states and INTERNATIONAL CRIMINAL COURTS — the most recent development in this law, described as vertical as against the HORIZONTAL cooperation between states (extradition, transit, mutual assistance, transfer for execution of sentence, transfer of proceedings, 'passive cooperation').

slides.title: Transnational criminal law and aut dedere aut iudicare
slides.text: The key elements of the treaties on crimes of a cross-border nature are THE OBLIGATIONS OF THE PARTIES TO CRIMINALISE THE PROHIBITED CONDUCT IN DOMESTIC LAW AND EITHER TO INVESTIGATE AND PROSECUTE OR TO EXTRADITE A SUSPECT APPREHENDED ON THEIR TERRITORY (AUT DEDERE AUT IUDICARE). Further typical elements are the facilitation of extradition by declaring the offences in question extraditable and EXCLUDING THE TRADITIONAL POLITICAL OFFENCE EXCEPTION. The treaty obligations apply ONLY INTER PARTES and cannot create jurisdictional titles opposable to third states beyond general international law. The practice begins with THREE MAJOR CONVENTIONS BETWEEN 1929 AND 1937: COUNTERFEITING OF CURRENCY, TRAFFIC IN NARCOTIC DRUGS AND TERRORISM (the last remaining a mere draft). Gradually SLAVERY, the slave trade, TRAFFICKING IN PERSONS, attacks on internationally protected persons, TORTURE, MONEY LAUNDERING, participation in ORGANISED CRIME, CYBERCRIME and CORRUPTION were added.

terms.def: Either extradite or prosecute — the obligation of the state on whose territory the suspect was apprehended.

cards.q: What are the key elements of the treaties on transnational crimes?
cards.a: The obligation of the parties to CRIMINALISE the prohibited conduct in domestic law and AUT DEDERE AUT IUDICARE — either to investigate and prosecute or to extradite a suspect apprehended on their territory. Plus the facilitation of extradition by declaring the offences extraditable and EXCLUDING THE POLITICAL OFFENCE EXCEPTION. The obligations apply only INTER PARTES.

cards.q: Which three crimes were covered by the first conventions of 1929–1937?
cards.a: Counterfeiting of currency, traffic in narcotic drugs and terrorism — the terrorism convention remaining a mere DRAFT. Only later were slavery, trafficking in persons, torture, money laundering, organised crime, cybercrime and corruption added.

slides.title: Protecting interests or values? The Hague model
slides.text: Kreß's careful analysis, worth having. Although many treaties speak in their preambles of 'CRIMES OF INTERNATIONAL CONCERN', A CLOSE READING OF THE OPERATIVE PROVISIONS SHOWS THAT LANGUAGE TO BE LOOSE. In multilateral treaties UP TO 1970 those provisions clearly evidence A CONCEPTION OF THE MUTUAL PROTECTION OF PARALLEL STATE INTERESTS, NOT THE PROTECTION OF FUNDAMENTAL VALUES OF THE INTERNATIONAL COMMUNITY — as can be seen from the fact that THE DUTY OF THE STATE OF APPREHENSION TO PROSECUTE DEPENDED ON THE RECEIPT AND REFUSAL OF AN EXTRADITION REQUEST from a state directly connected with the crime. A difficulty is posed by the 'HAGUE MODEL' of art. 7 of the CONVENTION FOR THE SUPPRESSION OF UNLAWFUL SEIZURE OF AIRCRAFT (1970), where the duty to prosecute NO LONGER DEPENDS ON A PRIOR EXTRADITION REQUEST AND ITS REFUSAL BUT APPLIES IN ALL CASES OF NON-EXTRADITION — and one might therefore say that this amounts to the recognition of a GENUINE VALUE OF THE INTERNATIONAL COMMUNITY. Supporting this is the preambular formula of most anti-terrorism conventions since 1973, that 'THE OCCURRENCE OF SUCH ACTS IS A MATTER OF GRAVE CONCERN TO THE INTERNATIONAL COMMUNITY AS A WHOLE'. BUT NEITHER IS DECISIVE. THE REAL TEST IS WHETHER STATES AGREE TO INTERNATIONALISE THE CRIMINAL NORM AND THEREBY CREATE A CRIME UNDER INTERNATIONAL LAW. So far it appears that, WITH THE SOLE EXCEPTION OF GRAVE BREACHES OF GENEVA CONVENTIONS I–IV, the 'Hague model crimes' have NOT CROSSED that threshold, and for conceptual clarity they should therefore be called TRANSNATIONAL CRIMES.

cards.q: Do the treaties on transnational crimes protect the values of the international community or the interests of states?
cards.a: Up to 1970 clearly THE INTERESTS OF STATES — the duty to prosecute depended on the receipt and refusal of an extradition request from a state connected with the crime. The Hague model (art. 7 of the 1970 hijacking convention) removed that condition, which would suggest recognition of a shared value. BUT THE REAL TEST IS WHETHER STATES AGREE TO INTERNATIONALISE THE NORM — and the 'Hague' crimes (except grave breaches of the Geneva Conventions) have not crossed that threshold.

slides.title: Piracy: why the 'classic example' is questionable
slides.text: In their separate opinion in the ARREST WARRANT case (DR CONGO v BELGIUM) Judges HIGGINS, KOOIJMANS AND BUERGENTHAL described piracy as the 'CLASSIC EXAMPLE' of a crime regarded 'AS MOST HEINOUS BY THE INTERNATIONAL COMMUNITY'. Kreß's response: THAT STATEMENT CAUSES SOME ASTONISHMENT. It should be self-evident that PIRACY, COMPARABLE IN GRAVITY TO ORDINARY ROBBERY, COMES NOWHERE NEAR THE HEINOUSNESS OF GENOCIDE OR CRIMES AGAINST HUMANITY — and it remains disputed whether piracy is a crime under international law at all. AT THE SAME TIME THE CUSTOMARY TITLE OF UNIVERSAL JURISDICTION OVER PIRACY ON THE HIGH SEAS IS UNDENIABLE — but it must be explained by SPECIAL CONSIDERATIONS. That SUI GENERIS position evidently rests on A COMBINATION OF TWO THINGS: THE ABSENCE OF A TERRITORIAL SOVEREIGN AND THE TYPICAL DIFFICULTY OF ESTABLISHING ANY OTHER TRADITIONAL BASIS OF JURISDICTION, especially the nationality of the alleged offender.

cards.q: Why is universal jurisdiction over piracy, on Kreß's view, an exception rather than a model?
cards.a: Because piracy is comparable in GRAVITY to ordinary robbery and comes nowhere near the heinousness of genocide; it is even disputed whether it is a crime under international law at all. The undeniable customary title of universal jurisdiction rests on a SUI GENERIS combination: THE ABSENCE OF A TERRITORIAL SOVEREIGN and the typical difficulty of establishing another jurisdictional title.

slides.title: International criminal law stricto sensu
slides.text: It establishes INDIVIDUAL CRIMINAL RESPONSIBILITY DIRECTLY UNDER INTERNATIONAL LAW; it protects THE FUNDAMENTAL VALUES OF THE INTERNATIONAL LEGAL COMMUNITY AS A WHOLE and expresses the IUS PUNIENDI of that community. ORIGINALLY THAT FUNDAMENTAL VALUE WAS INTERNATIONAL PEACE AND SECURITY; through more recent developments THE PROTECTION OF INTERNATIONALLY RECOGNISED HUMAN RIGHTS has also gained importance — the precise scope of that protection and the relation of the two values REMAINING TO BE DEFINED MORE CLEARLY. It may be expressed in treaties so as to satisfy the principle of legality in its strictest form, BUT IT MUST ULTIMATELY BE ANCHORED IN GENERAL INTERNATIONAL LAW, because it is inseparably bound up with the fundamental values of the community. This does not exclude the conceptual possibility of 'CRIMES UNDER INTERNATIONAL TREATY LAW': international criminal law stricto sensu may in time become THE HARD CORE OF A BROADER SUPRANATIONAL CRIMINAL LAW. SUPRANATIONAL CRIMINAL LAW NEED NOT BE UNIVERSAL — it may also arise where a treaty community of states PARTIALLY INTEGRATES THE EXERCISE OF ITS NATIONAL CRIMINAL JURISDICTIONS; the most likely candidate is the EUROPEAN UNION, BUT AS YET NO SUPRANATIONAL EUROPEAN CRIMINAL LAW EXISTS.

terms.term: ius puniendi of the international community
terms.def: The punitive power of the international community as a whole, expressed by international criminal law stricto sensu in protection of its fundamental values.

cards.q: What is international criminal law stricto sensu and what values does it protect?
cards.a: It establishes INDIVIDUAL CRIMINAL RESPONSIBILITY DIRECTLY UNDER INTERNATIONAL LAW and expresses the IUS PUNIENDI of the international community. Originally its value was INTERNATIONAL PEACE AND SECURITY; through more recent developments THE PROTECTION OF INTERNATIONALLY RECOGNISED HUMAN RIGHTS has also gained importance.

cards.q: What is supranational criminal law, and does a European one exist?
cards.a: It need not be universal: it may arise where a treaty community of states PARTIALLY INTEGRATES THE EXERCISE OF ITS NATIONAL CRIMINAL JURISDICTIONS. The most likely candidate is the European Union — BUT AS YET NO SUPRANATIONAL EUROPEAN CRIMINAL LAW EXISTS.

slides.title: The quarrel over Tadić and the Rome Statute
slides.text: International criminal courts sometimes RECOGNISE THE EXISTENCE OF CRIMES UNDER TREATY LAW TOO HASTILY — most notably the ICTY, which in PROSECUTOR v TADIĆ holds that individual criminal responsibility for war crimes can be derived from an existing humanitarian treaty provided the treaty norm binds both parties to the conflict. Kreß criticises this: THAT POSITION OVERLOOKS THE FACT THAT THE TREATIES IN QUESTION DO NOT THEMSELVES ESTABLISH INDIVIDUAL CRIMINAL RESPONSIBILITY — they do not create crimes under international treaty law — and IT IGNORES THE UNAMBIGUOUS MESSAGE OF THE SECRETARY-GENERAL'S REPORT on the establishment of the ICTY, that 'THE INTERNATIONAL TRIBUNAL SHOULD APPLY RULES OF INTERNATIONAL HUMANITARIAN LAW WHICH ARE BEYOND ANY DOUBT PART OF CUSTOMARY LAW'. Under the ROME STATUTE the situation differs in an important respect: ARTICLES 6 TO 8 formulate the crimes in such a way that THEY EXIST DIRECTLY UNDER THAT TREATY. Even so, the drafters shared the understanding that they were MERELY TO CODIFY OR AT MOST TO CRYSTALLISE INTERNATIONAL CRIMINAL LAW STRICTO SENSU, that is crimes under general international law, AND NOT TO CREATE NEW TREATY CRIMES. This is expressed by the preamble, which speaks of 'THE MOST SERIOUS CRIMES OF CONCERN TO THE INTERNATIONAL COMMUNITY AS A WHOLE', and still more clearly by the passage of the ELEMENTS OF CRIMES on crimes against humanity, under which art. 7 must be INTERPRETED STRICTLY and requires conduct 'IMPERMISSIBLE UNDER GENERALLY APPLICABLE INTERNATIONAL LAW, AS RECOGNIZED BY THE PRINCIPAL LEGAL SYSTEMS OF THE WORLD'. And an admission: ADHERING TO CUSTOMARY LAW PROVED DEMANDING, not least because of the dispute over HOW CUSTOM IS TO BE ASCERTAINED and because of THE LEGAL UNCERTAINTY OF ITS PRECISE CONTENT.

cards.q: What does Kreß object to in the ICTY's Tadić decision?
cards.a: That it derives individual criminal responsibility for war crimes from humanitarian treaties binding both parties to the conflict — thereby OVERLOOKING THAT THOSE TREATIES DO NOT THEMSELVES ESTABLISH INDIVIDUAL CRIMINAL RESPONSIBILITY, and ignoring the Secretary-General's instruction that the tribunal should apply only rules of humanitarian law BEYOND ANY DOUBT PART OF CUSTOMARY LAW.

cards.q: Did the Rome Statute create new crimes or merely codify?
cards.a: Formally its arts. 6–8 formulate the crimes so that they exist DIRECTLY UNDER THAT TREATY — but the drafters shared the understanding that they were MERELY TO CODIFY OR CRYSTALLISE international criminal law stricto sensu, not to create new treaty crimes. The preamble expresses this, as do the Elements of Crimes, under which art. 7 is to be interpreted STRICTLY.

slides.title: Features of the stricto sensu law: ius cogens and macrocriminality
slides.text: Contemporary international criminal law stricto sensu comprises GENOCIDE, CRIMES AGAINST HUMANITY, WAR CRIMES COMMITTED IN INTERNATIONAL AND NON-INTERNATIONAL ARMED CONFLICTS ALIKE, AND AGGRESSION. Criminal responsibility can be borne ONLY BY HUMAN BEINGS: THERE IS NO CRIMINAL RESPONSIBILITY OF LEGAL PERSONS AND IN PARTICULAR NO CRIMINAL RESPONSIBILITY OF THE STATE. International criminal law stricto sensu is IUS COGENS (non-derogable), it OVERRIDES ANY CONFLICTING NATIONAL LAW and likewise OVERCOMES THE TRADITIONAL STATE ENTITLEMENT TO IMMUNITY RATIONE MATERIAE. And the reason all three points are of fundamental practical importance: INTERNATIONAL CRIMINAL LAW STRICTO SENSU IS ESSENTIALLY CONCERNED WITH MACROCRIMINALITY DIRECTED OR SPONSORED BY A STATE LEADERSHIP. It may be enforced DIRECTLY by international jurisdictions or INDIRECTLY by states — and in the latter case THE NATIONAL JUDICIARY ACTS AS A TRUSTEE OF THE INTERNATIONAL IUS PUNIENDI. The jurisdiction of an international court may be PRIMARY OR COMPLEMENTARY to national ones, but IN CASE OF CONFLICT THE KOMPETENZ-KOMPETENZ MUST REMAIN WITH THE INTERNATIONAL COURT.

cards.q: What three properties does international criminal law stricto sensu have, and why are they of fundamental practical importance?
cards.a: It is IUS COGENS (non-derogable), it OVERRIDES conflicting national law and it OVERCOMES immunity ratione materiae. They are of fundamental practical importance because this law is essentially concerned with MACROCRIMINALITY DIRECTED OR SPONSORED BY A STATE LEADERSHIP — precisely those who would otherwise shelter behind their own law and immunity.

cards.q: Who can bear responsibility under international criminal law stricto sensu?
cards.a: ONLY HUMAN BEINGS. Under current international law there is NO CRIMINAL RESPONSIBILITY OF LEGAL PERSONS and in particular NO CRIMINAL RESPONSIBILITY OF THE STATE.

slides.title: Amnesties: from the Peace of Westphalia to the Rome Statute
slides.text: A particular challenge is the NATIONAL AMNESTY. From the WESTPHALIAN PEACE TREATIES OF 1648 a CONSISTENT PRACTICE OF INSERTING AN AMNESTY INTO PEACE TREATIES developed in Europe — and for KANT amnesty was even PART OF THE VERY IDEA OF MAKING PEACE. At first sight the TREATY OF VERSAILLES abandoned that practice, BUT IN THE LIGHT OF THE WAVE OF PARDONS AFTER THE FIRST AND — AS IS OFTEN FORGOTTEN — AFTER THE SECOND WORLD WAR TOO, one might argue that INTERNATIONAL CRIMINAL CASES, DESPITE THEIR OFTEN EMPHATIC BEGINNINGS, TEND TO END AS DE FACTO AMNESTIES. THE PREAMBLE OF THE ROME STATUTE recalls 'THAT IT IS THE DUTY OF EVERY STATE TO EXERCISE ITS CRIMINAL JURISDICTION OVER THOSE RESPONSIBLE FOR INTERNATIONAL CRIMES' — an evidently PRESCRIPTIVE formulation matching UN practice NOT TO ACCEPT AMNESTIES for crimes under international law, and supporting the emergence of A CUSTOMARY DUTY OF THE TERRITORIAL STATE TO INVESTIGATE OR PROSECUTE. BUT on a closer look at state practice the situation is MUCH MORE NUANCED, and THE STATUTE ITSELF DOES NOT EXPRESSLY PROHIBIT THE ADOPTION OF A NATIONAL AMNESTY — on the contrary, its provisions leave the organs of the Court room to respect such a decision. That in itself does not help much, BECAUSE NATIONAL DECISION-MAKERS NEED TO KNOW WHETHER AND ON WHAT CONDITIONS THE COURT WILL ACCEPT AN AMNESTY OR AN ALTERNATIVE RECONCILIATION SUCH AS A TRUTH COMMISSION OR NON-CRIMINAL SANCTIONS — and the urgent task is therefore to create legal certainty by developing criteria, which, given the variety of circumstances, is A DAUNTING TASK.

cards.q: How long is the European practice of amnesties in peace treaties, and what did the 20th century do to it?
cards.a: It runs from the WESTPHALIAN TREATIES OF 1648, and for Kant amnesty was part of the very idea of making peace. The Treaty of Versailles at first sight abandoned it, BUT IN THE LIGHT OF THE WAVE OF PARDONS AFTER BOTH WORLD WARS one may argue that international criminal cases TEND TO END AS DE FACTO AMNESTIES.

cards.q: Does the Rome Statute prohibit the adoption of a national amnesty?
cards.a: NOT EXPRESSLY — on the contrary, its provisions leave the Court's organs room to respect such a decision, although the preamble prescribes the duty of every state to exercise criminal jurisdiction over those responsible. The urgent task is therefore to develop CRITERIA so that national decision-makers know when the Court will accept an amnesty or a truth commission.

slides.title: Philosophical objections: Hegel, Kant, Rawls
slides.text: Three lines of criticism. THE HEGELIAN perspective essentially denies the existence of public international law and reduces it to EXTERNAL STATE LAW (ÄUSSERES STAATSRECHT) — from which international criminal law is a peculiar phenomenon, namely CRIMINAL LAW IN THE STATE OF NATURE. Such law is not necessarily illegitimate, but it differs strikingly from criminal law within a state; from that perspective it is argued (JAKOBS) that INTERNATIONAL CRIMINAL LAW IS NOT ABOUT REAFFIRMING AN EXISTING LEGAL ORDER BUT ABOUT CREATING A NEW ONE BY MEANS OF COERCION. Kreß rejects this: IT OVERSTATES THE EXISTING DIFFERENCES IN LAW ENFORCEMENT and overlooks the fact that the emerging system of international criminal justice itself strengthens certain vital components of the international order. THE KANTIAN line proceeds from 'TOWARDS PERPETUAL PEACE' (1795), where Kant questions the wisdom of subjecting states to a WORLD PUBLIC COERCIVE POWER. International criminal norms do not bind states as such, BUT THEY POSE A FORMIDABLE CHALLENGE TO THEIR SOVEREIGNTY, BECAUSE THEY ADDRESS THE SUBJECTS OF STATES DIRECTLY AND IRRESPECTIVE OF THEIR NATIONAL LAW — the system therefore necessarily contains AN EMBRYONIC ELEMENT OF THE WORLD PUBLIC ORDER KANT REJECTED. More recent Kantian writings do not deny legitimacy altogether and the dispute concerns the SCOPE: A MORE ORTHODOX APPROACH (KÖHLER) confines it to cases where the conduct DENIES THE VERY EXISTENCE OF AN INTERNATIONAL LEGAL PERSON OR OF A COMPONENT OF A STATE WITH THE POTENTIAL FOR LEGAL PERSONALITY (a national or ethnic group, say); THE MOST RECENT ATTEMPT (GIERHAKE) goes a decisive step further and accepts that it may extend to conduct which DENIES THE VERY IDEA OF HUMAN RIGHTS AS A PRECONDITION OF A WORLD ORDER OF PEACE. A THIRD OBJECTION: international criminal law places the individual in a CONFLICT OF DUTIES — he must choose between the SCYLLA of punishment for refusing a state order and the CHARYBDIS of criminal responsibility under international law for carrying it out. HOYER, on the basis of RAWLS'S THEORY OF JUSTICE, argued that for reasons of basic fairness the law should be CONFINED RATIONE PERSONAE TO THE LEADERSHIP OF A 'CRIMINAL STATE'. Kreß: such a categorical exclusion of everyone at lower levels GOES TOO FAR — the matter must be decided on the circumstances of the case, and in a genuine conflict the remedies range from MITIGATION OF SENTENCE to THE RECOGNITION OF A GROUND EXCLUDING RESPONSIBILITY. WITH THE SOLE EXCEPTION OF THE CRIME OF AGGRESSION, THE EXISTING LAW IS NOT A LAW OF LEADERS — though recent practice clearly concentrates on those bearing the greatest responsibility.

cards.q: What is the Hegelian objection to international criminal law, and how does Kreß reject it?
cards.a: That it is criminal law IN THE STATE OF NATURE, which does not reaffirm an existing legal order but creates a new one by coercion (Jakobs). Kreß objects that this OVERSTATES THE DIFFERENCES in law enforcement inside and outside the state, and that the emerging system of international criminal justice itself strengthens vital components of the existing international order.

cards.q: In what way is international criminal law a problem from the Kantian standpoint?
cards.a: Kant in 'Towards Perpetual Peace' (1795) questioned the wisdom of subjecting states to a world public coercive power. International criminal norms do not bind states, but they ADDRESS THEIR SUBJECTS DIRECTLY AND IRRESPECTIVE OF NATIONAL LAW — so the system necessarily contains AN EMBRYONIC ELEMENT OF THE WORLD PUBLIC ORDER Kant rejected.

cards.q: What is the 'conflict of duties' objection and how is it resolved?
cards.a: That the individual must choose between the Scylla of punishment for refusing a state order and the Charybdis of international criminal responsibility for carrying it out. Hoyer would confine the law, for fairness, to the LEADERSHIP of a 'criminal state'; Kreß rejects that as excessive and resolves the matter on the circumstances of the case — from MITIGATION OF SENTENCE to THE RECOGNITION OF A GROUND EXCLUDING RESPONSIBILITY. With the exception of aggression, the existing law is not a law of leaders.

slides.title: From Moynier to Nuremberg
slides.text: IN 1872 MOYNIER, the long-serving president of the INTERNATIONAL COMMITTEE OF THE RED CROSS, put forward THE FIRST PROPOSAL FOR AN INTERNATIONAL CRIMINAL COURT, to try violations of the Geneva Convention of 1864. But neither that proposal, nor the JOINT DECLARATION OF FRANCE, BRITAIN AND RUSSIA OF 24 MAY 1915 after the Armenian massacres, nor the Treaty of Versailles led to an international criminal jurisdiction — SO IT CAN HARDLY BE MAINTAINED THAT INTERNATIONAL CRIMINAL LAW STRICTO SENSU EXISTED AT THE TIME OF THE FIRST WORLD WAR. It became a live debate only in the INTERWAR PERIOD (the League of Nations, the Interparliamentary Union, the ILA, the Association Internationale de Droit Pénal). AFTER THE SECOND WORLD WAR the trials of the major war criminals before the NUREMBERG AND TOKYO tribunals were THE FIRST PRECEDENT of internationalised criminal proceedings. Institutionally they can hardly be portrayed as organs of the international community and as the first instance of direct enforcement; IN SUBSTANCE, HOWEVER, THEY MARKED A BREAKTHROUGH, BECAUSE THEY RECOGNISED THE EXISTENCE OF INTERNATIONAL CRIMINAL LAW STRICTO SENSU. The chief American motive for Nuremberg was the recognition that WAGING A WAR OF AGGRESSION IS A CRIME under international law; the tribunal's competence also covered war crimes and crimes against humanity — BUT FOR THE LATTER A DECISIVE LIMITATION APPLIED, THAT A CONNECTION WITH A WAR OF AGGRESSION OR A WAR CRIME HAD TO EXIST. FIRST-GENERATION INTERNATIONAL CRIMINAL LAW WAS THEREFORE INSEPARABLY TIED TO THE EXISTENCE OF WAR — reflecting the fact that at the time of Nuremberg international law focused almost exclusively on RELATIONS BETWEEN STATES.

cards.q: Did international criminal law stricto sensu exist at the time of the First World War?
cards.a: It can hardly be maintained: Moynier's 1872 proposal for an international criminal court, the joint declaration of France, Britain and Russia of May 1915 after the Armenian massacres, and the Treaty of Versailles all led to no international criminal jurisdiction. It became a live debate only in the INTERWAR PERIOD.

cards.q: How was Nuremberg a breakthrough, and what limitation did first-generation international criminal law have?
cards.a: Institutionally the tribunals can hardly be portrayed as organs of the international community, but IN SUBSTANCE THEY RECOGNISED THE EXISTENCE of international criminal law stricto sensu. The limitation: for crimes against humanity A CONNECTION WITH A WAR OF AGGRESSION OR A WAR CRIME HAD TO EXIST — the first-generation law was INSEPARABLY TIED TO THE EXISTENCE OF WAR.

slides.title: The long road through the UN system
slides.text: ON 11 DECEMBER 1946 the UN General Assembly affirmed the principles of international law recognised by the Nuremberg Charter and Judgment and directed their CODIFICATION; on the same day it affirmed that GENOCIDE, WHICH HAD NOT BEEN TRIED AT NUREMBERG AS A SEPARATE CRIME, is a crime under international law. Genocide was defined by the CONVENTION OF 9 DECEMBER 1948, BUT THE REST OF THE CODIFICATION TOOK ANOTHER ROAD: after the ILC's first drafts, the GA's legal committee decided in 1954 and again in 1957 TO POSTPONE ALL FURTHER WORK UNTIL AGREEMENT WAS REACHED ON AGGRESSION. IN 1978, four years after the 'ACT OF AGGRESSION' within the meaning of art. 39 of the Charter received a consensus definition (resolution 3314 of 1974), the committee recommended resuming the work; three years later the GA did so and mandated the ILC. The second phase led to the DRAFT CODES OF CRIMES AGAINST THE PEACE AND SECURITY OF MANKIND (1991 and 1996) and to the DRAFT STATUTE FOR AN INTERNATIONAL CRIMINAL COURT (1994), which became the basis of the ICC negotiations. And decisive momentum was given by the establishment of the ICTY IN 1993 AND THE ICTR IN 1994. Their fundamental significance is not diminished by the fact that both fall short of the ideal of a permanent court and had to bear the reproach of being 'AD HOC TRIBUNALS' established — at least in part — EX POST FACTO by the Security Council, A POLITICAL ORGAN WITH SELECTIVE MEMBERSHIP, and as its subsidiary organ. The subject-matter jurisdiction of both covers genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes — AND WHAT IS DECISIVE IS THAT BOTH REMOVED THE FIRST-GENERATION LAW'S TIE TO INTERNATIONAL ARMED CONFLICT: by crystallising war crimes committed in NON-INTERNATIONAL conflicts and by establishing crimes against humanity as A CLEARLY DISTINCT CATEGORY THAT CAN BE COMMITTED INSIDE OR OUTSIDE AN ARMED CONFLICT. The ICTY and ICTR thus CLEARED THE PATH FOR THE SECOND GENERATION of international criminal law, reflecting the intervening development of human rights.

cards.q: Why did the codification of international criminal law in the UN stall for decades?
cards.a: Because the General Assembly's legal committee decided in 1954 and again in 1957 TO POSTPONE ALL FURTHER WORK UNTIL AGREEMENT WAS REACHED ON AGGRESSION. Resumption was recommended only in 1978, four years after the consensus definition of an 'act of aggression' (resolution 3314 of 1974).

cards.q: How did the ICTY and ICTR clear the path for the second generation of international criminal law?
cards.a: They REMOVED THE TIE TO INTERNATIONAL ARMED CONFLICT: they crystallised war crimes committed in NON-INTERNATIONAL conflicts and established crimes against humanity as A CLEARLY DISTINCT CATEGORY that can be committed inside or outside an armed conflict. The second generation thereby reflects the intervening development of human rights.

slides.title: The ICC: the first permanent international criminal court
slides.text: After five sessions of the preparatory committee, the diplomatic conference in Rome adopted the STATUTE on 17 JULY 1998 by a large majority; with its entry into force on 1 JULY 2002 THE FIRST PERMANENT INTERNATIONAL CRIMINAL COURT IN LEGAL HISTORY came into being. The ICC is AN INDEPENDENT INTERNATIONAL LEGAL PERSON in the form of a new international judicial organisation. Its subject-matter jurisdiction reflects the development at the ICTY and ICTR and covers GENOCIDE, CRIMES AGAINST HUMANITY AND WAR CRIMES; it also covers the CRIME OF AGGRESSION, but THE EXERCISE OF THAT JURISDICTION WILL BE POSSIBLE ONLY ONCE THE CRIME HAS BEEN DEFINED. Personal jurisdiction is as a rule limited to persons who are either NATIONALS OF A STATE PARTY OR WHOSE CRIMES WERE ALLEGEDLY COMMITTED ON THE TERRITORY OF A STATE PARTY — but IT MAY BECOME TRULY UNIVERSAL IF THE SECURITY COUNCIL REFERS A SITUATION TO THE COURT. The ICC's jurisdiction is COMPLEMENTARY to national ones: THE COURT ACTS ONLY WHERE NO STATE IS WILLING OR ABLE GENUINELY TO CONDUCT PROCEEDINGS — and where the genuineness of national proceedings is disputed, THE ICC DECIDES CONCLUSIVELY. To these have been added domestic and mixed courts: the WAR CRIMES CHAMBER OF THE COURT OF BOSNIA AND HERZEGOVINA, the SPECIAL COURT FOR SIERRA LEONE, the SPECIAL PANELS IN DILI (EAST TIMOR) and the EXTRAORDINARY CHAMBERS IN THE COURTS OF CAMBODIA. The consensus that perpetrators should not go unpunished is therefore, in the words of the opinion cited, 'BEING PURSUED THROUGH A FLEXIBLE STRATEGY IN WHICH THE NEWLY ESTABLISHED INTERNATIONAL TRIBUNALS, TREATY OBLIGATIONS AND NATIONAL COURTS ALL HAVE THEIR PART TO PLAY'.

terms.def: The ICC acts only where no state is willing or able genuinely to conduct proceedings; where the genuineness is disputed, the Court decides conclusively.

cards.q: What is the subject-matter and personal jurisdiction of the ICC?
cards.a: Subject matter: genocide, crimes against humanity, war crimes — and the crime of aggression, whose exercise, however, is possible only after its definition. Personal: as a rule persons who are NATIONALS OF A STATE PARTY or whose crimes were committed ON THE TERRITORY OF A STATE PARTY — but it may become UNIVERSAL if the Security Council refers a situation to the Court.

cards.q: What does the complementarity of ICC jurisdiction mean?
cards.a: That the ICC acts ONLY WHERE NO STATE IS WILLING OR ABLE GENUINELY TO CONDUCT PROCEEDINGS — and where the genuineness of national proceedings is disputed, the Court itself decides conclusively (the Kompetenz-Kompetenz remains with the international court).

slides.title: The great powers outside the Court and the tension of the age
slides.text: The consensus that perpetrators should not go unpunished DOES NOT MEAN CONSENSUS ON THE SHAPE OF THE SYSTEM: CHINA, INDIA, RUSSIA AND THE USA remain outside the ICC. The American government would have preferred a court DEPENDENT ON REFERRAL BY THE SECURITY COUNCIL and questions the international legality of the jurisdictional framework. Under the presidency of G. W. Bush it sought to curtail the jurisdiction further in order to shield its soldiers effectively: it forced through SECURITY COUNCIL RESOLUTION 1422 (2002), a legally questionable instrument which FORBADE THE COURT TO EXERCISE JURISDICTION OVER NATIONALS OF NON-PARTY STATES ACTING UNDER A COUNCIL MANDATE under Chapter VII. The resolution was valid for a year and, OWING TO GROWING OPPOSITION, WAS RENEWED ONLY ONCE — whereupon the USA turned to building A NETWORK OF BILATERAL AGREEMENTS. Kreß sets this in a wider frame: the Bush administration's opposition shows THE ENDURING DIFFICULTY OF THE ICC IN REALISING ITS VISION OF COMPLETE EQUALITY BEFORE THE LAW, and MORE FUNDAMENTALLY REFLECTS A CHARACTERISTIC FEATURE OF THE PRESENT EPOCH OF INTERNATIONAL LAW: THE TENSION BETWEEN THE UNPRECEDENTED ASPIRATIONS OF THE INTERNATIONAL COMMUNITY AND THE STRONG HEGEMONIC TEMPTATION OF THE 'LONELY SUPERPOWER'. It is hopeful that the USA has occasionally relented: on 31 MARCH 2005 the Security Council adopted RESOLUTION 1593, referring the SITUATION IN DARFUR to the Court — and the USA, instead of vetoing, CHOSE TO ABSTAIN. It is not an enthusiastic affirmation of universality and equality, but a gesture that ENABLED RATHER THAN OBSTRUCTED THE COURT'S WORK — and for the first time THE POTENTIAL OF COMPLEMENTARY ACTION BY THE SECURITY COUNCIL AND THE ICC became visible.

cards.q: What was Security Council resolution 1422 (2002) and what became of it?
cards.a: A legally questionable instrument forced through by the USA: it FORBADE the ICC to exercise jurisdiction over nationals of NON-PARTY STATES acting under a Security Council mandate under Chapter VII. It was valid for a year and, OWING TO GROWING OPPOSITION IN THE COUNCIL, WAS RENEWED ONLY ONCE — the USA then turned to building a network of bilateral agreements.

cards.q: What feature of the present epoch of international law does US opposition to the ICC reflect, on Kreß's account?
cards.a: THE TENSION BETWEEN THE UNPRECEDENTED ASPIRATIONS OF THE INTERNATIONAL COMMUNITY AND THE STRONG HEGEMONIC TEMPTATION OF THE 'LONELY SUPERPOWER'. A hopeful counter-movement was that on resolution 1593 (2005) referring Darfur the USA CHOSE TO ABSTAIN rather than veto — and the potential of complementary action by the Council and the Court became visible for the first time.

slides.title: The principle of legality: from jurisdictional title to written law
slides.text: The charters of the Nuremberg and Tokyo tribunals and the statutes of the ICTY and ICTR referred to crimes under international law essentially ONLY AS TITLES OF JURISDICTION — to establish the FULL DEFINITION the judges had to turn TO CUSTOMARY LAW. THE ROME STATUTE DEPARTS FROM THAT PRACTICE and in arts. 6 to 8 DEFINES genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes. That decisive step towards LEX SCRIPTA is complemented by ART. 22, which excludes proceedings for crimes other than those the Statute enumerates and defines — and THE UNPRECEDENTED EMPHASIS ON THE PRINCIPLE OF LEGALITY is underlined further by the adoption of the ELEMENTS OF CRIMES, which 'SHALL ASSIST THE COURT IN THE INTERPRETATION AND APPLICATION OF ARTICLES 6, 7 AND 8' (art. 9(1)).

cards.q: How did the Rome Statute depart from the practice of the earlier tribunals on the principle of legality?
cards.a: The earlier charters and statutes referred to the crimes only AS TITLES OF JURISDICTION, and judges had to find the full definition in CUSTOMARY LAW. The Rome Statute DEFINES the crimes in arts. 6–8 (lex scripta), art. 22 excludes proceedings for other crimes, and the adoption of the ELEMENTS OF CRIMES (art. 9(1)) underlines that unprecedented emphasis on legality.

slides.title: Genocide and crimes against humanity
slides.text: The definition of GENOCIDE in art. 6 comes from art. 2 of the Genocide Convention. THE ESSENCE OF THE CRIME LIES IN THE INTENT TO DESTROY, IN WHOLE OR IN PART, A NATIONAL, ETHNICAL, RACIAL OR RELIGIOUS GROUP. And a practical refinement: that intent PRACTICALLY SPEAKING REFERS TO A COLLECTIVE GENOCIDAL CAMPAIGN, because a lone individual will not, save in the most exceptional circumstances, be able to FORM A REALISTIC INTENT TO BRING ABOUT AT LEAST THE PARTIAL DESTRUCTION OF A GROUP BY HIS OWN CONDUCT. The ICTR and ICTY significantly clarified the definition and the INTERNATIONAL COURT OF JUSTICE essentially confirmed their case law in its judgment in BOSNIA AND HERZEGOVINA v SERBIA AND MONTENEGRO (2007) — but important questions about the delimitation of the protected groups, about the notion of 'PART OF A GROUP' and about the 'INTENT TO DESTROY' REMAIN THE SUBJECT OF INTENSE DISPUTE. ART. 7 IS THE FIRST CODIFICATION OF CRIMES AGAINST HUMANITY. It is today settled customary law that a crime against humanity can — like genocide — be committed INSIDE OR OUTSIDE AN ARMED CONFLICT. Its essence lies in the requirement that THE CONDUCT OF THE INDIVIDUAL PERPETRATOR (murder, torture, rape and others) MUST FORM PART OF A WIDESPREAD OR SYSTEMATIC ATTACK DIRECTED AGAINST ANY CIVILIAN POPULATION, WITH KNOWLEDGE OF THAT ATTACK. The main challenge is to define that CONTEXTUAL ELEMENT as clearly as possible, because it is by that threshold element THAT THE SUBSTANTIVE SCOPE OF THE WHOLE OF INTERNATIONAL CRIMINAL LAW STRICTO SENSU IS DEFINED. And here Kreß approves a departure: ART. 7(2) RIGHTLY REJECTS THE MORE RECENT, OVER-PROGRESSIVE CASE LAW OF THE ICTY AND INSISTS ON THE REQUIREMENT OF A STATE OR ORGANISATIONAL POLICY BEHIND THE COLLECTIVE ACTIVITY — although the precise definition of 'policy' and 'organisation' remains to be clarified.

cards.q: What is the essence of genocide and why does it refer to a collective campaign?
cards.a: THE INTENT TO DESTROY, IN WHOLE OR IN PART, A NATIONAL, ETHNICAL, RACIAL OR RELIGIOUS GROUP. Practically, that intent refers to A COLLECTIVE GENOCIDAL CAMPAIGN, because a lone individual will not — save in the most exceptional circumstances — be able to form a realistic intent to bring about at least the partial destruction of a group BY HIS OWN CONDUCT.

cards.q: What is the essence of a crime against humanity and what is its most disputed element?
cards.a: The conduct of the individual perpetrator (murder, torture, rape) MUST FORM PART OF A WIDESPREAD OR SYSTEMATIC ATTACK AGAINST A CIVILIAN POPULATION, WITH KNOWLEDGE OF THAT ATTACK. The most disputed is that CONTEXTUAL ELEMENT, because it defines the substantive scope of the whole of international criminal law stricto sensu — and art. 7(2), unlike the more recent ICTY case law, insists on the REQUIREMENT OF A STATE OR ORGANISATIONAL POLICY.

slides.title: War crimes: the oldest, and yet disputed until 1945
slides.text: War crimes are often regarded as the OLDEST CRIMES under international law; the traditional notion is tied to INTERSTATE WAR and has its root in the traditional law of war, which in the second half of the 19th century became the subject of progressive regulation by international conventions, which in turn gave rise to a growing body of customary law. Originally 'war crime' denoted A VIOLATION OF THE LAWS AND CUSTOMS OF WAR, often with the addition that it must be SERIOUS. THE POWER OF A BELLIGERENT TO PUNISH WAR CRIMES OF PERSONS ON THE OTHER SIDE — either by direct application of the law of war or under national criminal law — WAS RECOGNISED BY 1907, when HAGUE CONVENTION IV came into being. BUT — and this is the point — THE EXISTENCE OF WAR CRIMES UNDER INTERNATIONAL LAW REMAINED DISPUTED UNTIL THE END OF THE SECOND WORLD WAR. Today the customary law of war crimes in international conflicts is well established: besides Hague Convention IV the main points of reference are GENEVA CONVENTIONS I–IV and ADDITIONAL PROTOCOL I (1977). The Geneva Conventions follow the tradition of 'GENEVA LAW', that is the protection of persons hors de combat; Additional Protocol I combines Geneva elements with RULES ON THE CONDUCT OF HOSTILITIES, which traditionally belonged to the separate 'HAGUE LAW'. ART. 8(2)(a) of the Statute takes over the provisions on GRAVE BREACHES of the Geneva Conventions, (b) defines war crimes of Hague origin — and because Additional Protocol I is not yet universally accepted, MANY FORMULATIONS IN (b) ARE TAKEN FROM HAGUE CONVENTION IV OF 1907.

terms.def: Geneva law protects persons hors de combat; Hague law regulates the conduct of hostilities. Additional Protocol I (1977) combines the two.

cards.q: Are war crimes the oldest category, and since when have they been uncontested?
cards.a: They are often regarded as the oldest, and the power of a belligerent to punish the other side's crimes was recognised by 1907 (Hague Convention IV). BUT THE EXISTENCE OF WAR CRIMES UNDER INTERNATIONAL LAW REMAINED DISPUTED UNTIL THE END OF THE SECOND WORLD WAR.

cards.q: Distinguish Geneva and Hague law and say how this is reflected in art. 8 of the Rome Statute.
cards.a: GENEVA LAW protects persons HORS DE COMBAT; HAGUE LAW regulates the CONDUCT OF HOSTILITIES (Additional Protocol I of 1977 combines the two). Art. 8(2)(a) takes over the GRAVE BREACHES of the Geneva Conventions, (b) defines crimes of HAGUE origin — and because Protocol I is not universally accepted, many formulations in (b) are taken from Hague Convention IV of 1907.

slides.title: War crimes in non-international conflict and Tadić
slides.text: The crystallisation of war crimes committed in NON-INTERNATIONAL armed conflict is one of the most important aspects of the turbulent development since the 1990s. The problem: COMMON ARTICLE 3 OF THE GENEVA CONVENTIONS CONTAINS NO GRAVE BREACHES REGIME like the one for international conflict, and the same is true of ADDITIONAL PROTOCOL II (1977). When the ICTY and ICTR were established there was therefore CONSIDERABLE DOUBT WHETHER WAR CRIMES IN NON-INTERNATIONAL CONFLICTS EXISTED UNDER INTERNATIONAL LAW AT ALL. This explains the LANDMARK SIGNIFICANCE OF THE TADIĆ DECISION OF 2 OCTOBER 1995, in which the existence of customary war crimes in non-international conflicts was CONFIRMED together with a FAR-REACHING ASSIMILATION of their regulation to the settled law of international conflicts. The Rome Statute essentially confirms this: ART. 8(2)(c) AND (e) contain TWO LISTS of war crimes in non-international conflict, the second of which also reaches into the field of the CONDUCT OF HOSTILITIES. (And note the tension: on the source of individual responsibility Kreß criticises the Tadić decision, while here he acknowledges its landmark significance.)

cards.q: Why was the Tadić decision of 1995 a landmark for war crimes?
cards.a: Because neither common art. 3 of the Geneva Conventions nor Additional Protocol II contains a grave breaches regime, so the existence of war crimes in NON-INTERNATIONAL conflicts was disputed. Tadić CONFIRMED their customary existence together with a FAR-REACHING ASSIMILATION to the law of international conflicts — and the Rome Statute confirmed this in art. 8(2)(c) and (e) with two lists.

slides.title: Aggression: a historical irony
slides.text: Unlike the statutes of the ICTY and ICTR, the Rome Statute's list includes the CRIME OF AGGRESSION — and the Statute acknowledges in its preamble that PEACE AND SECURITY IN THE WORLD ARE THE SUPREME COLLECTIVE VALUE THE COURT IS TO PROTECT. It thereby supports the view that aggression IS a crime under international law, as the BRITISH HOUSE OF LORDS unanimously confirmed IN 2006 (R v JONES). PARADOXICALLY, HOWEVER, FOR WANT OF AN AGREED DEFINITION THE COURT CANNOT EXERCISE ITS JURISDICTION OVER THAT CRIME. And Kreß names it precisely: THAT JUDICIAL INCAPACITY IS A HISTORICAL IRONY IN THE LIGHT OF THE FACT THAT THE NUREMBERG TRIBUNAL CALLED THE WAGING OF A WAR OF AGGRESSION 'THE SUPREME INTERNATIONAL CRIME'. The drafters were aware that this definitional gap left their Rome work unfinished, and the Statute therefore CALLS FOR ITS OWN COMPLETION by entrusting states with a mandate to define the crime. The three most important points in the negotiations of the SPECIAL WORKING GROUP: the formulation of the EXCLUSIVELY LEADERSHIP NATURE of the crime; the precise definition of THE STATE USE OF ARMED FORCE as a necessary precondition of individual responsibility; and THE PROCEDURAL ROLE TO BE GIVEN TO THE SECURITY COUNCIL. The last is 'THE QUESTION OF QUESTIONS', BECAUSE IT SETS THE PRINCIPLE OF EQUALITY BEFORE THE LAW AGAINST THE POWERFUL POLITICAL DEMANDS OF THE FIVE PERMANENT MEMBERS OF THE COUNCIL.

cards.q: What is the historical irony about the crime of aggression?
cards.a: That the Rome Statute includes it and recognises peace and security as the supreme protected value — but FOR WANT OF AN AGREED DEFINITION THE COURT CANNOT EXERCISE JURISDICTION OVER IT. And this although THE NUREMBERG TRIBUNAL CALLED THE WAGING OF A WAR OF AGGRESSION 'THE SUPREME INTERNATIONAL CRIME'.

cards.q: Which three questions had to be settled by the definition of aggression, and which is the 'question of questions'?
cards.a: The formulation of the EXCLUSIVELY LEADERSHIP NATURE of the crime; the precise definition of THE STATE USE OF ARMED FORCE as a precondition of individual responsibility; and THE PROCEDURAL ROLE OF THE SECURITY COUNCIL. The last is the 'question of questions' because it SETS THE PRINCIPLE OF EQUALITY BEFORE THE LAW AGAINST THE POWERFUL POLITICAL DEMANDS OF THE FIVE PERMANENT MEMBERS.

slides.title: Terrorism: a third generation?
slides.text: After 11 SEPTEMBER 2001 a debate flared up about transnational terrorism and the Rome Statute — AND IT IS OF AN ENTIRELY DIFFERENT ORDER FROM THE DEBATE ABOUT AGGRESSION. The debate on aggression concerns THE COMPLETION OF THE CODIFICATION OF THE SECOND GENERATION; the debate on terrorism asks WHETHER CERTAIN VIOLENT ACTS COMMITTED BY PRIVATE (ATERRITORIAL) ACTORS ACROSS BORDERS SHOULD BE CRIMINALISED DIRECTLY UNDER GENERAL INTERNATIONAL LAW — that is, whether A THIRD GENERATIONAL STEP is in prospect. It would mean the law moving into the field of CONFLICTS BETWEEN STATES AND DESTRUCTIVE PRIVATE ORGANISATIONS: its protective reach, so far confined to war and internal unrest, would extend to THE PROTECTION OF STATES AND THEIR POPULATIONS AGAINST EXTERNAL THREATS OF A MAGNITUDE COMPARABLE TO FOREIGN AGGRESSION BUT EMANATING FROM PRIVATE PERSONS. Many take it for granted that conduct such as the attacks of 11 September already falls within the ICC's subject-matter jurisdiction: the American strategy of the 'WAR ON TERROR' (re)conceives them as WAR CRIMES, while the prevailing doctrine holds that they may amount to CRIMES AGAINST HUMANITY. Kreß warns: against a thinly supported obiter dictum of one ICTY chamber it is HARD TO DEMONSTRATE THAT THE CUSTOMARY LAW OF CRIMES AGAINST HUMANITY HAS DEVELOPED TO THAT POINT — and it is SERIOUSLY DISPUTED whether violent transnational private organisations NOT CONTROLLING STATE TERRITORY belong among the entities the Statute recognises as possible authors of a policy of attack against a civilian population. Supporting evidence: WHEN THE SPECIAL TRIBUNAL FOR LEBANON WAS ESTABLISHED, THE SECRETARY-GENERAL'S FAR-REACHING PROPOSAL TO INCLUDE CRIMES AGAINST HUMANITY IN ITS JURISDICTION WAS REJECTED BY THE SECURITY COUNCIL.

cards.q: Why is the debate on terrorism of a different order from the debate on aggression?
cards.a: Aggression concerns THE COMPLETION OF THE SECOND-GENERATION CODIFICATION. Terrorism asks whether violent acts by PRIVATE (ATERRITORIAL) ACTORS across borders should be criminalised directly under general international law — that is, whether A THIRD GENERATIONAL STEP is in prospect, extending the protective reach from war and internal unrest to external threats of the magnitude of aggression emanating from private persons.

cards.q: Do attacks such as those of 11 September fall under crimes against humanity?
cards.a: Kreß is sceptical: against a thinly supported obiter dictum of an ICTY chamber it is HARD TO DEMONSTRATE that customary law has developed to that point, and it is SERIOUSLY DISPUTED whether private organisations NOT CONTROLLING STATE TERRITORY can be authors of a 'policy' of attack. Supporting this: when the Special Tribunal for Lebanon was established, the Security Council REJECTED the proposal to include crimes against humanity.

slides.title: The general part: the first in history, and still raw
slides.text: The statutes of the ICTY and ICTR regulate general principles only RUDIMENTARILY — an eclectic list of forms of responsibility plus provisions on superior orders and on COMMAND RESPONSIBILITY. PART 3 OF THE ROME STATUTE, by contrast, regulates many general principles in detail and IS THE FIRST ATTEMPT IN THE HISTORY OF INTERNATIONAL CRIMINAL LAW TO FORMULATE A GENERAL PART OF SUBSTANTIVE CRIMINAL LAW. It shows the drafters' determination TO TRANSCEND THE BIAS OF LEGAL FAMILIES — in Rome they deliberately avoided terminology with too strong a connotation of one family. Even so, the analytical distinction between 'MATERIAL ELEMENTS' (ACTUS REUS), 'MENTAL ELEMENTS' (MENS REA) and 'GROUNDS EXCLUDING RESPONSIBILITY' (DEFENCES) IS A LEGACY OF THE HISTORICAL PREDOMINANCE OF THE COMMON LAW. The most important feature is A HEIGHTENED SENSITIVITY TO THE PRINCIPLE OF GUILT AND THE REQUIREMENT OF SUBJECTIVE ATTRIBUTION — whereas in the ICTY's case law there are traces of a strong EMPHASIS ON PREVENTION, not only in sentencing but ALREADY IN FORMULATING THE CONDITIONS OF RESPONSIBILITY. The most striking example is the joint opinion of Judges McDONALD AND VOHRAH in ERDEMOVIĆ (1997), where they denied the availability of the defence of DURESS to a war crime of intentional killing, invoking the need to promote the effectiveness of humanitarian law. And the Rome Statute vindicated the dissenters: ART. 31(1)(d) lists necessity as a ground excluding responsibility AND CONTAINS NO EXCEPTION FOR INTENTIONAL KILLING AND MURDER. The Statute further recognises, within limits, EXCUSABLE MISTAKE OF LAW BASED ON A SUPERIOR ORDER and mistakes that NEGATE THE MENTAL ELEMENT of a crime. All this shows that THE DRAFTERS GAVE PRECEDENCE TO THE PRINCIPLE OF INDIVIDUAL GUILT WHERE ITS OUTCOME APPEARS TO CONFLICT WITH PREVENTION. At the same time many components look LIKE RAW CRIMINAL-LAW MATERIAL — the provision on necessity, for instance, which does not distinguish A JUSTIFICATION FROM AN EXCUSE, or the undifferentiated treatment of several forms of command responsibility. Part 3 will therefore require JUDICIAL REFINEMENT with thorough comparative analysis — and it offers 'THE BEST POSSIBLE INCENTIVE TO DIG DEEP AND TO FORMULATE THE „GRAMMAR“ OF MODERN INTERNATIONAL CRIMINAL LAW'.

cards.q: What makes Part 3 of the Rome Statute unique, and what in it nevertheless remains tied to one legal family?
cards.a: It is THE FIRST ATTEMPT IN HISTORY to formulate a GENERAL PART of substantive international criminal law, with a deliberate effort to avoid the terminology of one legal family. Even so, the distinction between 'material elements' (actus reus), 'mental elements' (mens rea) and 'grounds excluding responsibility' (defences) IS A LEGACY OF THE HISTORICAL PREDOMINANCE OF THE COMMON LAW.

cards.q: How did the Rome Statute resolve the dispute over duress from the Erdemović case?
cards.a: In favour of the DISSENTING judges: art. 31(1)(d) lists necessity as a ground excluding responsibility AND CONTAINS NO EXCEPTION FOR INTENTIONAL KILLING AND MURDER — whereas Judges McDonald and Vohrah had denied that defence by invoking the need for prevention. It shows that the drafters gave PRECEDENCE TO THE PRINCIPLE OF INDIVIDUAL GUILT OVER PREVENTION.

slides.title: Procedure: the prosecutor as a seeker of truth, and the role of victims
slides.text: Proceedings before the ICTY and ICTR clearly followed the ADVERSARIAL MODEL OF THE COMMON LAW (with the single exception of evidence): responsibility for establishing the truth lies chiefly with 'the prosecution' and 'the defence', and although the degree of judicial intervention grew over time, the model did not change. At the ICC, by contrast, a multilateral process compelled CONCESSIONS FROM THE WHOLE SPECTRUM OF LEGAL FAMILIES, and after more than ten years a procedural regime emerged with UNIQUE COMPROMISES and an unprecedented complexity of sources. Proceedings run in the order: PRELIMINARY ANALYSIS OF A SITUATION, INVESTIGATION, CONFIRMATION HEARING, TRIAL and possibly APPEAL AND REVISION (in a broad conception also ENFORCEMENT). The most significant departures: UNLIKE THE STATUTES OF THE ICTY AND ICTR, THE ROME STATUTE REQUIRES THE PROSECUTOR TO INVESTIGATE INCRIMINATING AND EXONERATING CIRCUMSTANCES EQUALLY — the drafters thus gave him THE ROLE OF A SEEKER OF TRUTH MORE LIKE AN OFFICER OF JUSTICE THAN A PARTISAN ADVOCATE. The interplay of the prosecutor and the PRE-TRIAL CHAMBER is SUI GENERIS: the pre-trial judges have supervisory functions placing them SOMEWHERE BETWEEN A GERMAN ERMITTLUNGSRICHTER AND A FRENCH JUGE D'INSTRUCTION. The confirmation hearing at the ICTY and ICTR was held EX PARTE, whereas at the ICC IT TAKES PLACE IN THE PRESENCE OF THE ACCUSED AND HIS COUNSEL — and it copies no national solution but combines elements of several systems. It remains an open question whether THE JUDGES HAVE A DUTY TO ESTABLISH THE TRUTH PROPRIO MOTU — it is not expressly included. And a novelty: ON THE ROLE OF VICTIMS THE CASE LAW OF THE EARLIER TRIBUNALS IS OF LITTLE HELP, because the Statute conceives RESTORATIVE JUSTICE ANEW — VICTIMS HAVE A FAR-REACHING RIGHT TO PARTICIPATE IN THE PROCEEDINGS AND A RIGHT TO REPARATIONS ON AN INDIVIDUAL OR COLLECTIVE BASIS.

cards.q: How does the prosecutor's role at the ICC differ from the ICTY and ICTR?
cards.a: The Rome Statute requires him to INVESTIGATE INCRIMINATING AND EXONERATING CIRCUMSTANCES EQUALLY — the drafters thus gave him THE ROLE OF A SEEKER OF TRUTH LIKE AN OFFICER OF JUSTICE, not a partisan advocate. At the ICTY and ICTR the adversarial common law model applied, where the parties are responsible for establishing the truth.

cards.q: What novelty does the Rome Statute bring for victims?
cards.a: It conceives RESTORATIVE JUSTICE anew: victims have A FAR-REACHING RIGHT TO PARTICIPATE IN THE PROCEEDINGS and A RIGHT TO REPARATIONS on an individual or collective basis. The case law of the earlier tribunals is of little help here.

slides.title: Cooperation: the weakest link
slides.text: Without a view of the 'EXTERNAL PART' of the procedure — the law of cooperation between the Court and states — one cannot understand how the ICC will function. Those rules govern THE SURRENDER OF PERSONS to the Court, the forms of cooperation in PROVIDING EVIDENCE and, in a broader conception, THE ENFORCEMENT OF SENTENCES. And the reason this matters so much: ANY INTERNATIONAL CRIMINAL COURT WILL REMAIN 'UTTERLY POWERLESS' (CASSESE) WITHOUT THE COOPERATION OF STATES AND IN THE ABSENCE OF ITS OWN ENFORCEMENT APPARATUS — and a former ICTY judge called the lack of state cooperation 'THE MOST FRUSTRATING ASPECT' of international criminal justice. PART 9 of the Statute therefore substantially SHORTENS THE LIST OF GROUNDS on which states may refuse requests, does not exclude on-site investigations and entrusts the Court with deciding AUTHORITATIVELY on states' obligations — thereby remaining within the logic of VERTICAL cooperation set out in the BLAŠKIĆ case. At the same time, however, the cooperation regime SUFFERS FROM SERIOUS WEAKNESSES, CAUSED RATHER BY STATES' CONCERNS FOR SOVEREIGNTY THAN BY A DETERMINATION TO PROTECT HUMAN RIGHTS. For the surrender of suspects the main gap is THE ABSENCE OF AN EXPRESSLY STATED POWER TO ENFORCE SURRENDER BY INTERNATIONAL ARMED FORCES within a peace operation. For the other forms THE COURT LACKS THE POWER TO REQUIRE STATES TO COMPEL WITNESSES TO APPEAR BEFORE IT, and the power to investigate on site is narrowly defined. And finally: THE CONVOLUTED COMPROMISE ON INFORMATION RELATING TO NATIONAL SECURITY can hardly be called instructed by the Blaškić case, which showed that ALLOWING A STATE'S UNILATERAL ASSERTION OF NATIONAL SECURITY AND ITS REFUSAL TO PRODUCE DOCUMENTS CAN PARALYSE INTERNATIONAL CRIMINAL PROCEEDINGS. The cooperation provisions may therefore, on Kreß's view, be the first thing in the new procedural regime to NEED URGENT AMENDMENT.

cards.q: Why is state cooperation the weakest link of international criminal justice?
cards.a: Because ANY INTERNATIONAL CRIMINAL COURT WILL REMAIN 'UTTERLY POWERLESS' (Cassese) WITHOUT THE COOPERATION OF STATES AND WITHOUT ITS OWN ENFORCEMENT APPARATUS — a former ICTY judge called the lack of cooperation 'the most frustrating aspect' of this justice.

cards.q: Name the weaknesses of the cooperation regime under the Rome Statute.
cards.a: There is no expressly stated power to ENFORCE THE SURRENDER of suspects by international armed forces in a peace operation; the Court CANNOT REQUIRE STATES TO COMPEL WITNESSES to appear before it; on-site investigation is narrowly defined; and the convoluted compromise on NATIONAL SECURITY information repeats, uninstructed, the problem from the Blaškić case. The weaknesses stem rather from CONCERNS FOR SOVEREIGNTY than from the protection of human rights.

slides.title: Looking ahead
slides.text: Kreß closes with the famous sentence of the Nuremberg Tribunal: 'CRIMES AGAINST INTERNATIONAL LAW ARE COMMITTED BY MEN, NOT BY ABSTRACT ENTITIES, AND ONLY BY PUNISHING INDIVIDUALS WHO COMMIT SUCH CRIMES CAN THE PROVISIONS OF INTERNATIONAL LAW BE ENFORCED.' DURING THE COLD WAR THAT SENTENCE WENT UNANSWERED; IT WAS RECALLED ONLY IN THE 1990s, and with the entry into force of the Rome Statute in 2002 it can at last be ACTED UPON CONSISTENTLY. The ICC signals that THE APPLICATION OF INTERNATIONAL CRIMINAL LAW STRICTO SENSU, THOUGH OF PRACTICAL NECESSITY IT WILL REMAIN SELECTIVE, MAY IN FUTURE BE FAR LESS HAPHAZARD THAN IN THE PAST. And a final recommendation, surprising in such a text and therefore memorable: AFTER THE TURBULENT RENAISSANCE AND DEVELOPMENT OF THE 1990s THERE IS NO URGENT NEED TO PUSH THE BOUNDARIES OF INTERNATIONAL CRIMINAL LAW FURTHER — INSTEAD, THE GREAT ACHIEVEMENT OF ESTABLISHING THE ICC MUST BE CONSOLIDATED AND STRENGTHENED.

cards.q: Quote the sentence of the Nuremberg Tribunal on which Kreß builds his conclusion, and say what became of it.
cards.a: 'Crimes against international law are committed by MEN, NOT BY ABSTRACT ENTITIES, and only by punishing individuals who commit such crimes can the provisions of international law be enforced.' During the Cold War it went unanswered; it was recalled only in the 1990s and can be acted upon consistently since the entry into force of the Rome Statute in 2002.

cards.q: What does Kreß recommend as the next step?
cards.a: Surprisingly NOT further expansion: after the turbulent renaissance of the 1990s THERE IS NO URGENT NEED TO PUSH THE BOUNDARIES OF INTERNATIONAL CRIMINAL LAW FURTHER — the great achievement of establishing the ICC must be CONSOLIDATED AND STRENGTHENED.
